Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Mapping functional versatility and fragility of Ras GTPase signaling circuits through in vitro network reconstitution" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor (Phil Cole) and Tony Hunter as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers (Mark Philips, Mike Rosen, and Shu-Ou Shan) have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The authors present an ingenious study of signal processing down the Ras pathway. These investigators develop an exceedingly simple yet powerful system: measure the recruitment in vitro to Ras-coated microbeads of fluorescently tagged Ras binding domains (RBDs) of various effectors to quantify the amplitude and kinetics of Ras signaling. By manipulating the density, mutational or GTP-binding state of the bound Ras along with the concentrations of single or multiple GEFs, GAPs and effectors, the investigators are able to observe a wide variety of signal outputs. Among the most compelling results is the dependence on GAP concentrations of the difference in signal output between wt and activated Ras (Figure 3). This type of in vitro systems approach to Ras signaling provides much fodder for discussion and future investigation and contributes to our understanding of how a single pathway with a small number of nodes can generate a wide-variety of outputs. In addition, the manuscript is clearly written and the graphically didactic and uniform figures help make an inherently dense set of data digestible. Accordingly, the manuscript is suitable for publication in eLife. However, it is recommended that several issues be addressed.

Essential revisions:

1) The manuscript would be deeper and ultimately more satisfying if the phenomena could be explained in terms of the biochemical properties of the component species (rate constants, binding affinities, etc.). It might be said that the majority of observations from Figures 1–6 can be predicted from a simple molecular model using only four free parameters: (i) the rate constant of GDP -> GTP exchange to generate GTP-bound Ras; (ii) the rate constant of GTP hydrolysis to generate GDP-bound Ras; (iii) and (iv), the rate constants for effector binding to and dissociating from GTP-bound Ras. Different responses were observed because each of these parameters can be changed by modulating concentration, introducing allostery or competition. Furthermore, this modeling should take into account predicted cellular concentrations of the various components. Constructing such a model and comparing the predictions (a simple kinetic simulation) with the empirical data observed here will significantly enhance the value of this work, and any deviations from the prediction will suggest new mechanisms or biology. Most of the explanations in the text for individual pieces of data will likely also be folded into this more fundamental, organizing model.

2) While no new experiments are requested on this point, discussion is needed on how the absence of membranes in this system may alter the interpretation of the results. Ras proteins are peripheral membrane proteins that, although they appear to stably associate with membranes at steady state, are, in fact, in a dynamic equilibrium both in terms of association with the membrane per se (see PMID 16236799) and within membrane microdomains (see PMID: 17618274). The behavior of the stationary Ras proteins affixed to the inert microbeads is likely quite different from their membrane-asociated counterparts in an in vivo system. The lack of membrane also confounds other aspects of interpreting the results. For example, in their analysis the authors equate recruitment of the RBD of an effector to the microbead as a readout of signaling. But this is simplistic. Raf-1 is a kinase that is the first node in a cascade of kinases. The sine qua non of Raf-1 signaling involves stimulation of the kinase activity of Raf-1. Yet the interaction of Raf-1 with GTP-loaded Ras does not stimulate kinase activity in the absence of a cellular membrane (PMID: 8622647, 7811320). Indeed, the membrane acts upon the Raf-1 kinase in a manner that involves the cysteine-rich domain and initiates a poorly understood activation sequence, which may include dimerization. Importantly, Raf-1 sent to the membrane via a CAAX sequence does not require GTP•Ras at all for full activation (PMID: 8196769, 7811320) demonstrating that it is membrane not Ras that activates the kinase. Likewise GEFs for Ras and other small GTPases require biological membranes for activation. Indeed, the way GEFs like SOS and RasGRPs are regulated is by modulation of their affinity for membranes utilizing domains like SH2 (on Grb2), PH and C1 for membrane binding. Although the catalytic domain of SOS will have exchange activity toward Ras in solution, in vivo the histone, PH and DH domains are required for productive associate with membranes (PMID: 20133692).

3) We could not find information about sample size and statistical analysis of data. This needs to be laid out clearly.

claims.source: Indeed, the output dynamics from allosteric-feedback networks appeared much more stable and monotonic than those from RasGRF networks that contained no feedback.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing SOScat and RasGRF systems.

claims.claim: For a RasGRF GEF step-input, the system experiences a sudden increase in catalytic activity all at once; for SOScat GEF, this step-input in protein levels becomes a ramp-input in terms of protein activity.
claims.source: These differences in comparison to the RasGRF-RBD positive feedback system can be at least partially attributed to the OFF→ON feedback mechanism of SOScat in the context of a step-input: for a RasGRF GEF step-input, the system experiences a sudden increase in catalytic activity all at once; for SOScat GEF, although, this step-input in protein levels becomes a ramp-input in terms of protein activity because it takes multiple rounds of GEF activity to produce enough Ras•GTP for SOScat to achieve significant activity (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of SOScat activation, illustrated in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: A single signaling system like Ras can encode multiple dynamic signal processing behaviors by regulating the concentration and identity of network components.
claims.source: Our experiments imply that, much in the same way that a single genome can encode multiple cell types that are regulated through differential gene expression, a single signaling system like Ras can encode multiple dynamic signal processing behaviors by regulating the concentration and identity of network components.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of diverse outputs from different network configurations.

claims.claim: There is a staggering amount of diversity in what types of network configurations are present in different cell types and tissues based on p120GAP, Ras, and c-Raf mRNA expression levels.
claims.source: For example, a simple survey of published p120GAP, Ras, and c-Raf mRNA expression levels across a variety of tissue types reveals a staggering amount of diversity in what types of network configurations are present in different cell types and tissues (Figure 9A, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from Genevestigator shown in Figure 9A and Table 1.

claims.claim: The versatility of Ras systems comes with a trade-off of fragility, as there exist numerous paths to altered signaling behaviors that could cause disease.
claims.source: This versatility is not without trade-offs, however. In particular, we observed many different paths in network-space from one signaling processing behavior to another with much higher or sustained amplitude (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations, illustrated in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: The same flexibility that allows Ras systems to realize many different signaling behaviors creates many opportunities for misregulation in response to perturbation.
claims.source: Thus, the same flexibility that allows Ras systems to realize many different signaling behaviors creates many opportunities for misregulation in response to perturbation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of multiple paths to altered signaling.

claims.claim: Network configurations that produced highly similar output behaviors could nonetheless respond divergently to perturbations.
claims.source: Even networks configurations that produced highly similar output behaviors could nonetheless respond divergently to perturbations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of phase diagrams.

claims.claim: Binding to activated Ras is a physiological prerequisite for other regulatory mechanisms to take place for Raf kinases.
claims.source: However, this only further emphasizes the importance of effector binding dynamics in the context of cellular signal processing, as binding to Ras is a physiological prerequisite for these other mechanisms to take place.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Raf regulation.

claims.claim: Intrinsic hydrolysis by H-Ras continues to occur even in the presence of saturating amounts of effector.
claims.source: This result is consistent with previous observations that intrinsic hydrolysis by the GTPase continues to occur even in the presence of saturating amounts of effector (Herrmann et al., 1995).

claims.source: NF1-GAP, which is expressed somewhat ubiquitously but highest in neuronal cells and leukocytes, has a tight KM for Ras (0.3 μM) and modest kcat (1.4 s-1) (Wiesmüller and Wittinghofer, 1992).

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published biochemical characterization.

claims.claim: A-Raf has lower affinity for Ras•GTP (koff = 5.52x10-4 s-1, kon = 7.20x103 M-1s-1) than C-Raf (koff = 2.15x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.02x104 M-1s-1).
claims.source: To this end, we purified and labeled RBDs from the A-Raf and B-Raf kinases, which have lower (koff = 5.52x10-4 s-1, kon = 7.20x103 M-1s-1) and higher (koff = 1.48x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.32x104 M-1s-1) affinities for Ras•GTP than C-Raf (koff = 2.15x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.02x104 M-1s-1), respectively (Fischer et al., 2007), to examine the signal processing behavior of two-effector systems in either GAP-free or high NF1-GAP networks.

claims.source: To this end, we purified and labeled RBDs from the A-Raf and B-Raf kinases, which have lower (koff = 5.52x10-4 s-1, kon = 7.20x103 M-1s-1) and higher (koff = 1.48x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.32x104 M-1s-1) affinities for Ras•GTP than C-Raf (koff = 2.15x10-4 s-1, kon = 1.02x104 M-1s-1), respectively (Fischer et al., 2007), to examine the signal processing behavior of two-effector systems in either GAP-free or high NF1-GAP networks.

results.result: The authors developed a microscopy-based bead reconstitution assay that enables multi-turnover, real-time tracking of Ras signaling dynamics by monitoring fluorescent effector recruitment to Ras-loaded beads in response to GEF and GAP inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23 collectively demonstrate successful development and validation of the assay system. The experimental data (C21-C23, C67-C70) show GTP-dependent effector translocation, dose-dependent responses to GEF and GAP, and multi-turnover cycling capability. The methodological details (C60, C65) and controls establish the system's validity.

results.result: Oncogenic G12V Ras mutation produces minimal signal distortion in GAP-free networks but causes dramatic sustained signaling (>40-fold higher steady state) in high-GAP networks, with maximal perturbation occurring under low-GEF/high-GAP conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 provide direct experimental evidence showing context-dependent effects of G12V mutation. The phase diagram analysis (C30) systematically maps distortion across network configurations. The data demonstrate that GAP/GEF balance critically determines oncogenic impact, supporting the main conclusion (C4).

results.result: Modeling suggests that transient overshoot behavior in wild-type Ras systems requires either competition between effectors and GAPs or a post-hydrolysis refractory GTPase state, with the three-state model best explaining experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 present a logical progression from theoretical constraint (two-state systems cannot overshoot) through mechanistic hypotheses to model validation. The modeling data (C33) demonstrates that the three-state model with physiological parameters captures key experimental features including differential WT vs G12V behavior.

results.result: NF1-GAP concentration modulates both steady-state amplitude and dynamic shape of effector outputs, with increasing GAP levels producing lower steady states, transient overshoot behavior, and inversely correlated pulse-width and peak-time.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 describe consistent experimental observations of NF1-GAP effects on system dynamics. The biochemical characterization (C61) provides context for interpreting these effects. The data demonstrate systematic, dose-dependent modulation of multiple output features.

results.result: p120GAP has weaker effects on steady-state effector output compared to NF1-GAP, but still modulates output dynamics in a dose-dependent manner, consistent with its higher KM and kcat.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 presents experimental comparison showing differential GAP effects. The biochemical parameters (C62) provide mechanistic explanation for observed differences. The weaker effect is consistent with higher KM reducing effective GAP activity at tested concentrations.

results.result: Ras density directly correlates with effector output amplitude, while lower Ras densities produce increasingly transient responses, suggesting a switch from Ras-excess to GEF-excess regimes.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 describe systematic experimental observations across Ras density ranges. The data show both amplitude and dynamic changes, with mechanistic interpretation supported by the authors' kinetic modeling. The density estimation method is acknowledged as approximate but sufficient for comparative analysis.

results.result: Higher effector concentrations increase output amplitude and enable capture of more transient features of upstream Ras•GTP dynamics, indicating effectors actively interpret rather than passively transmit Ras signals.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 presents experimental data showing concentration-dependent effects on both amplitude and dynamics. Claim C41 provides a mechanistic interpretation supported by the data and modeling. The conclusion that effectors play an active interpretive role is a reasonable inference from the observed concentration-dependent kinetic effects.

results.result: The concentration and identity of network components (GEF, GAP, Ras, effectors) strongly impact timing, duration, shape, and amplitude of outputs, enabling a single Ras system to encode multiple dynamic behaviors through differential component expression.
results.evaluation: This integrative result synthesizes findings from multiple parameter scans. Claims C3 and C53 are supported by the comprehensive experimental mapping across 96 network configurations and the demonstration of diverse output behaviors. The analogy to differential gene expression creating cell types is conceptually sound.

results.result: Different Raf effectors (A-Raf, B-Raf, C-Raf) with distinct binding kinetics interpret the same Ras input with different output dynamics, enabling temporal multiplexing where a single input encodes multiple temporally distinct outputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 provide experimental evidence of differential effector responses in both GAP-free and high-GAP contexts. The binding kinetics data (C63-C64) provide mechanistic basis. Claim C45 draws a reasonable inference about temporal organization of signaling. The competition mechanism (C42) is supported by modeling.

results.result: Point mutations in effectors can dramatically alter output dynamics, making new dynamic patterns readily accessible during evolution.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by experimental data showing C-Raf N64A mutant behavior differs from wild-type. The modeling also demonstrates that small parameter changes can shift timing. The evolutionary accessibility argument is a reasonable inference from the ease of generating new dynamics through single mutations.

results.result: Recruitment-based positive feedback (RasGRF-RBD fusion) is particularly effective at amplifying weak signals in high-GAP/low-GEF network contexts, with strongest effects when GAP activity dominates intrinsic GEF activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 describe systematic experimental observations across 96 network configurations with feedback. The phase diagram analysis quantifies feedback gain across parameter space. The mechanistic interpretation (localized GEF activity overcoming GAP dominance) is consistent with the data.

results.result: Allosteric feedback (SOScat) does not provide large amplitude gains but minimizes transient overshoot, producing more stable monotonic responses by converting step inputs in protein levels to ramp inputs in activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 present experimental observations of SOScat effects across network configurations. The mechanistic explanation (C52) for differences from RasGRF-RBD feedback is a reasonable inference based on SOScat's OFF→ON activation mechanism (C66). The overshoot minimization is consistently observed in the data.

results.result: Expression levels of p120GAP, Ras, and c-Raf show substantial diversity across different cell types and tissues based on mRNA expression data.
results.evaluation: Claim C54 is supported by Genevestigator data presented in Figure 9A and Table 1. The analysis appropriately uses published expression data to demonstrate natural variation in network configurations. However, mRNA levels may not perfectly reflect protein levels or activities.

results.result: The versatility of Ras systems comes with fragility, as multiple paths exist to altered signaling behaviors through mutations, expression changes, or network perturbations, with similar network configurations potentially responding divergently to perturbations.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 present inferences from the comprehensive experimental mapping. The phase diagrams demonstrate multiple paths to high-amplitude signaling and show that similar outputs can arise from different configurations. The fragility argument is a logical consequence of the observed versatility and is illustrated in Figure 9C.

results.result: Ras GTPases function as molecular switches cycling between GTP-bound (ON) and GDP-bound (OFF) states, with GEFs promoting activation and GAPs promoting inactivation, playing central roles in cell proliferation and morphology with disease associations when mutated.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C12 present established background knowledge about Ras biology, supported by appropriate citations to foundational literature. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of Ras function and regulation. This background contextualizes the experimental work.

results.result: Traditional in vitro Ras assays monitor single-turnover events under non-cycling conditions, failing to capture signaling dynamics that are critical for cellular responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15 accurately describe limitations of conventional biochemical assays, supported by citations to methods literature. Claim C16 establishes the importance of dynamics. These claims effectively motivate the need for the multi-turnover system developed in this work.

results.result: Different effectors interpret the same inputs with distinct output dynamics, enabling multiple unique temporal outputs in response to a single input.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 is a high-level summary supported by the detailed multi-effector experiments (C42-C46). This represents a key conceptual advance demonstrating temporal multiplexing in Ras signaling. The claim is well-supported by experimental data showing differential C-Raf, B-Raf, and A-Raf responses.

results.result: Binding to activated Ras is a physiological prerequisite for downstream Raf regulation, and intrinsic hydrolysis continues even with saturating effector present.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 represents established knowledge about Raf regulation. Claim C59 is supported by citation and is consistent with the experimental observations of effector decay in GAP-free conditions (C67). These claims provide important context for interpreting effector binding dynamics.
